summary:
The Confirmation Of Congressional Observer Access Act of 2024 (COCOA Act) amends the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (HAVA) to require States to provide designated congressional election observers full access to observe all elements of election administration procedures for federal elections. The Act inserts a new section 304 into Title III of HAVA (52 U.S.C. 21081 et seq.), redesignating existing sections 304 and 305 as sections 305 and 306, respectively, and makes conforming amendments to the enforcement provision and table of contents.

New section 304(a) states a finding that Congress possesses constitutional authority under Article I, section 5, clause 1 and Article I, section 4, clause 1 to send observers, and that the section’s procedures do not establish new authorities but provide a convenient statutory reference. Subsection (b) requires each State to give a designated congressional election observer “full access to clearly observe all elements of election administration procedures,” including access to any area where a ballot is cast, processed, scanned, tabulated, canvassed, recounted, audited, or certified, during pre- and post-election procedures. The observer may not handle ballots or election equipment, advocate for a position or candidate, reduce ballot secrecy or voter privacy, interfere with a voter or election administrator, or otherwise disrupt the process. Subsection (b)(3) clarifies that an observer may ask questions of election officials.

Subsection (c) governs removal. A state or local election official who has a reasonable basis to believe an observer has engaged in or imminently will engage in intimidation, deceptive practices prohibited by federal law, or disruption of voting, processing, scanning, tabulating, canvassing, recounting, or certification may remove the observer. The official must, within 24 hours, inform the chair and ranking minority member of the relevant congressional committee (the Committee on House Administration or the Committee on Rules and Administration) and provide written notice of the reasons for removal. Mere presence of an observer, without additional indicia, is not a sufficient basis for removal. If an observer is properly removed, the chair or ranking minority member may send a replacement observer for the remainder of the observation period.

Subsection (d) defines “designated congressional election observer” as a House or Senate employee designated in writing by the chair or ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration or the Committee on Rules and Administration (or a successor committee) to gather information about an election, including for contested election purposes. Subsection (e) defines “State” to include the 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.

The Act amends section 401 of HAVA (52 U.S.C. 21111) by adding “304” to the list of sections subject to the enforcement provision, thereby making the access requirement enforceable by the Attorney General. The Act contains no separate authorization of appropriations or delayed effective date; it took effect upon enactment on October 4, 2024.
